meta.title: Lunar vs Solar Eclipses — Follow the Shadow

design.visualThesis: Moving shadows make the two alignments instantly distinguishable.
design.motionGrammar: Orbital movement, moving shadow cones, continuous solar transit, curved light rays; no static-slide substitutes.
design.assetLanguage: Original SVG planetary illustrations with shading and craters. No external imagery. Diagrams labeled not to scale.

scenes.narration: One hides the Sun. The other turns the Moon red. Here's the difference.
scenes.visual: Twin disks: Moon crosses the Sun while a second Moon darkens to copper.

scenes.narration: In a solar eclipse, the Moon moves between the Sun and Earth. Its shadow falls on a small part of Earth.
scenes.visual: Moon moves into Sun-Earth alignment; its narrow shadow meets Earth.

scenes.narration: From that shadow, the Moon can cover the Sun. During totality, the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, becomes visible.
scenes.visual: Large Moon disk crosses the solar disk; corona appears at complete coverage.

scenes.narration: In a lunar eclipse, Earth sits between the Sun and Moon. The Moon travels through Earth's shadow.
scenes.visual: Earth remains central while Moon moves into its shadow cone.

scenes.narration: During a total lunar eclipse, some sunlight bends through Earth's atmosphere. More red light reaches the Moon, giving it a copper glow.
scenes.visual: Warm light paths curve around Earth and reach a Moon that changes from gray to copper.

scenes.narration: Why not every month? The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so the shadows usually miss.
scenes.visual: Moon follows a tilted orbital track and misses the extended shadow axis.

scenes.narration: Solar: the Moon's shadow on Earth. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon. For solar viewing, use proper eclipse glasses, never ordinary sunglasses.
